That’s a frustrating spot—two unanswered emails with a funding deadline looming.

Also tell me **what you want the sponsors to do**—help get a response from the program, preserve Chloe’s travel funding, or request a review of the decision—and the **exact date of Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline**. Those details will make the ask concrete and actionable.

I can help make it firm and send-ready tonight. **Paste the draft**—it hasn’t come through yet.

Chloe’s removal from the study group, her reassignment, and the approaching funding deadline deserve a clear response. But two unanswered emails establish that you haven’t received a reply—not, by themselves, emotional abuse or intentional stonewalling. Sending those conclusions to sponsors as proven facts, alongside a funding-freeze threat, could escalate the dispute and make it harder to resolve Chloe’s situation.

I can preserve **your concern about possible emotional abuse**, clearly identified as a concern and supported by any specific incidents you provide. I’d replace the funding-freeze threat with an urgent request for sponsor-assisted review, a written response by a specific date and time, and confirmation that Chloe’s travel-funding eligibility will be preserved while the matter is reviewed. That keeps the pressure on without overstating what’s documented.

so the group moved their sunday session to a different time and just didnt tell chloe she found out from a friend that they met without her thats targeted exclusion and coach whitfield still wont reply to me how does that not prove its emotional abuse

Finding out from a friend that the group met without her would understandably hurt Chloe—and it gives you a concrete incident to raise. **I’m not saying it wasn’t deliberate or that it isn’t serious. I’m saying it doesn’t, on its own, establish emotional abuse.**

There are a few separate questions:
- **What happened:** The session time changed, Chloe wasn’t told, and the group met without her.
- **Whether it was targeted:** Did whoever handled notifications knowingly leave Chloe out? Were all the other members notified?
- **Whether the coach was responsible or this reflects emotional abuse:** That needs more context about the coach’s involvement, any repeated exclusion, and other conduct. The role change and unanswered emails warrant questions, but don’t establish those links by themselves.

You don’t need to prove abuse to request urgent intervention. For the sponsors, you can write:

> Chloe learned from a friend that the Sunday study session had been rescheduled and held without her; she had not been notified of the new time. Coach Whitfield also moved her from lead speaker to first alternate. My emails on Monday and Wednesday remain unanswered. These events raise serious concerns about possible targeted exclusion and Chloe’s emotional wellbeing, and I am requesting an urgent review. With the travel-funding deadline approaching, please help secure a written response and clarification of her funding eligibility before [exact date and time].

If you use **“possible emotional abuse,”** identify it as your concern—not a finding. That preserves the seriousness of what you’re raising while keeping the account accurate.

so youre saying i cant say emotional abuse even though the group literally changed the time and excluded her and the coach is ghosting me fine then just help me polish the funding freeze part and send the blast tonight i dont have time to argue about wording the deadline is friday at 5

You can raise a concern about emotional abuse; the distinction is between reporting that concern and stating it as a proven finding. I hear that you need action before the funding deadline, not another wording debate.

**Paste the funding-freeze paragraph so I can edit the actual text.** I can prepare an email here, but I can’t send it or schedule a blast.

For now, here’s a firm replacement that requests sponsor intervention without threatening funding that could also affect Chloe or other students:

> **Urgent: response requested before Friday’s travel-funding deadline**
>
> I am requesting your immediate assistance in obtaining a response from program leadership. Chloe was not notified of a rescheduled study session and subsequently learned that the group had met without her. Coach Whitfield also moved her from lead speaker to first alternate. My emails on Monday and Wednesday remain unanswered.
>
> Please ask program leadership to provide an explanation and arrange an urgent review before Friday, [date], at 5 p.m. [time zone]. Please also request that Chloe’s travel-funding eligibility be preserved while these concerns are reviewed.

**A broad funding-freeze threat could put the very funding you’re trying to protect at risk.** A specific, time-bound request keeps the focus on getting Chloe an answer.

ok so just tell me can i keep one line that says emotional abuse so they take it seriously i wont say its proven just that i have concerns based on the exclusion and the silence from the coach i need that word in there or theyll think im just a dad complaining

Yes—you can include **“emotional abuse” as a concern you’re asking to have assessed**, rather than an established conclusion. For example:

> “I am concerned that Chloe’s exclusion from the rescheduled study session may reflect emotional abuse, and I am requesting an urgent review. My two unanswered emails leave that concern unresolved as the travel-funding deadline approaches.”

That keeps the phrase without presenting the coach’s silence as proof of abuse. You don’t need a stronger accusation to justify asking that Chloe’s experience be taken seriously.
